title: A Creative Practice
summary: Build a capture system, use incubation and routines, beat blocks and complete a small portfolio project.
objectives: Set up a capture system for ideas.
Plan a small portfolio project with a finish date.

explanation.heading: Creativity as a habit
explanation.body: Creative people are not waiting for lightning; they have habits that make ideas likely and catch them when they come. A creative practice has four parts: capture ideas, give them time to develop, keep going when stuck and produce visible work. This lesson turns the techniques you have learned into a routine you can keep for years.

explanation.heading: Capture system
explanation.body: Ideas are fragile. You have a thought in the shower and it is gone by breakfast. A **capture system** is one place, always within reach, where every idea goes: a notes app, a pocket notebook or voice memos. Rules: one place only, write it immediately, no editing while capturing. Once a week spend ten minutes reviewing, tagging the promising ones and deleting the rest. Review is what turns a pile of scraps into a resource. Add small context to each note, such as where it came from and why it excited you. A bare note reading "app idea" is useless in a month, while "app idea: queue tracker for the canteen, from waiting 25 minutes today" can be developed immediately.

explanation.heading: Incubation and routines
explanation.body: **Incubation** means stepping away from a problem so that your mind keeps working in the background. Work hard on a problem, then walk, shower, sleep or do something unrelated. Insight often arrives during the break. For this to work you must first immerse yourself in the problem. Pair it with a **routine**: the same time and place each day, a short warm-up and a clear start signal such as making tea. Even 30 minutes daily beats a rare eight-hour session. Protect the slot like an appointment. On low-energy days, do a smaller version, such as five minutes, rather than skipping, because keeping the chain unbroken matters more than the length of the session.

explanation.heading: Beating blocks and building a portfolio
explanation.body:
When stuck, try these: lower the bar ("write the worst version"), change the medium or location, set a five-minute timer, impose a constraint, work on a different part, or show someone a rough draft. Blocks often come from perfectionism and fear of judgement, not lack of ideas.

A **portfolio project** is a small, finished, shareable piece that shows your ability: a mini web app, a case study or a short guide. Keep it small enough to finish in two weeks. Define the audience, the scope and the finish date, build in public view if you can, and write a short note about what you learned. For a student targeting a first job, two or three small finished projects count for more than many half-built ones.

examples.title: A capture habit
examples.body: Kavita keeps a pocket notebook. On Sunday she reviews it, stars three notes and moves two into a project list. One starred note became a college blog series.
examples.takeaway: Capture plus weekly review turns scraps into projects.

examples.title: A small portfolio piece
examples.body: Sameer builds a tiny expense tracker in ten days, deploys it and writes a one-page note about design choices. He adds it to his resume as evidence of finishing.
examples.takeaway: A small finished project is evidence of ability.

exercises.why: One reliable place prevents losing ideas.

exercises.prompt: Stepping away from a problem so that your mind keeps working on it is called ____. (one word)
Plan a small portfolio project you could finish in two weeks. State what it is, the audience, the scope (what is in and out), the finish date and how you will share it.

descriptors.3: Small with clear in and out.
Named and linked to the project value.

exercises.modelAnswer: Project: a small SAP ABAP learning log site with ten short posts. Audience: other beginners and recruiters. In scope: ten posts, one summary page. Out of scope: comments and login. Finish date: 28 October. Share: post on LinkedIn and add it to my resume.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans are small, give a date and name where it will be shown. Avoid projects that need months.

exercises.prompt: You have stared at a blank page for twenty minutes. What helps most?

options.text: Set a five-minute timer and write the worst possible version.
options.feedback: Lowering the bar starts the flow.

exercises.why: Lower the bar and start small.

task.title: Set up your practice
task.brief: Create a capture system and plan a small portfolio project.
steps: Choose one capture tool and add ten ideas today.
Schedule a 30-minute daily creative slot at a fixed time.
Plan one small project with scope and a finish date.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your tool, slot time and project finish date.

quiz.why: Finished small projects are better evidence than large unfinished ones.

reflection: What is the smallest daily creative habit you could keep for a month, and at what time will you do it?

keyPoints: Capture every idea in one place.
Finish a small project to show your work.
